Infection Control & Asepsis

Chain of infection, hand hygiene, PPE, standard precautions and aseptic technique.

🎯 After this chapter you can

  • Describe the chain of infection
  • Demonstrate correct hand hygiene
  • Explain standard precautions and PPE use

In simple words

Infection control means preventing germs from spreading to patients, staff and visitors. The chain of infection shows how infection spreads — and where we can break it.

Asepsis means being free from germs. Medical asepsis (clean technique) reduces germs; surgical asepsis (sterile technique) removes all germs.

Chain of infection

Link Meaning How to break it
Infectious agent The germ Kill the germ
Reservoir Where it lives Clean the source
Portal of exit How it leaves Cover coughs, dispose of waste
Mode of transmission How it spreads Hand hygiene, PPE
Portal of entry How it enters Protect wounds, sterile technique
Susceptible host The person at risk Vaccinate, good nutrition

Hand hygiene

The single most important way to prevent infection. Wash with soap and water when hands are visibly dirty; use alcohol-based hand rub otherwise.

Five moments of hand hygiene:

  1. Before touching a patient.
  2. Before a clean/aseptic procedure.
  3. After body fluid exposure risk.
  4. After touching a patient.
  5. After touching patient surroundings.

Standard precautions & PPE

Treat every patient’s blood and body fluids as potentially infectious. Use PPE:

  • Gloves — for contact with blood/body fluids.
  • Mask — protects nose and mouth.
  • Gown — protects clothing.
  • Goggles/face shield — protects eyes.

🔴 Hand hygiene is #1

Hand hygiene is the single most important way to prevent infection. Use the five moments; wash with soap when visibly dirty, otherwise use hand rub.

Where the nurse uses this

  • Hand hygiene — before and after every patient contact and before clean procedures.
  • PPE — wear gloves, mask and gown as needed; remove carefully and dispose safely.
  • Sharps safety — never recap needles; drop in a puncture-proof container.
  • Waste segregation — colour-coded bins; infectious waste goes in yellow bags.
  • Isolation — follow the precautions on the isolation sign outside the room.

🔴 Most important for exams

  1. Chain of infection: germ, source, exit, spread, entry, host.
  2. Break any link to stop infection spread.
  3. Hand hygiene is the single most important preventive measure.
  4. Five moments of hand hygiene — before touch, before clean procedure, after body fluids, after touch, after surroundings.
  5. Standard precautions: treat all blood and body fluids as infectious.

⭐ Important for exams

  1. PPE: gloves, mask, gown, goggles or face shield.
  2. Never recap needles; use a puncture-proof container.
  3. Surgical asepsis = sterile technique; medical asepsis = clean technique.

📌 Memory trick

Five moments: “T-B-A-A-A” — Before Touch, Before clean procedure, After body fluids, After touch, After surroundings.

60-second revision

  • Chain of infection: germ → source → exit → spread → entry → host.
  • Break any link to stop spread.
  • Hand hygiene = most important preventive measure.
  • Five moments of hand hygiene.
  • Standard precautions = treat all blood/fluids as infectious.
  • PPE: gloves, mask, gown, goggles.

Test yourself

The single most important way to prevent infection is:

Answer: B. Hand hygiene is the single most important measure to prevent infection spread.

Standard precautions mean:

Answer: B. Standard precautions treat every patient's blood and body fluids as potentially infectious.

Used needles should be:

Answer: B. Never recap needles; drop them directly into a puncture-proof sharps container.

The portal of entry is:

Answer: C. Portal of entry is how the germ gets into a new person (e.g., a wound).

Medical asepsis means:

Answer: B. Medical asepsis (clean technique) reduces the number of germs; surgical asepsis removes all germs.
